parsed.attack: Home-inventory and house-record apps have existed for twenty years, have been actively promoted by insurers who benefit from them, and have never sold, because the buyer must act during a period of zero felt pain and the payoff arrives during an emergency. That asymmetry is sharper here: when the pressure tank fails at 11pm with water on the floor, a rural well-and-septic owner does not want a part number, they want the well guy's mobile number, and the well guy arrives with the part. A first-time rural owner does not yet know which fittings will matter, so the photographs they take will not be the ones they need; an owner who does know has already stopped needing the app. The evidence offered is three failed products and an argument about what Google Lens structurally cannot do - a supply-side gap, not a single instance of a homeowner asking for or paying for this.
parsed.strongest_defence: First-time rural buyers are inside a well-documented spending window in the first 90 days of ownership, when they are anxious about systems they have never had before and are buying water tests, filters and service contracts; $25 once at that moment is an impulse, not a considered purchase, and the exportable house sheet gives it a second life at resale.
parsed.verdict_reason: Two decades of proven non-adoption for structurally identical products is hard behavioural evidence against the pain being felt at purchase time, though the new-owner anxiety window is a real and narrow exception.
